_comment: Diplomat's mesh model — the deployment overlay SzpontNet merges over its own netmodel.json (szpontnet-core/szpontnet/netmodel.json, the canonical v1 constants). This half is what both front-ends RENDER: the duty catalog (which job classes the mesh routes, with per-duty platform spread — e.g. the audit's one-linux-plus-one-macos), the placement strategies, the platform/token/trust vocabularies and the tier labels. Wire constants and the quota accounting model are the node's business and live in netmodel.json; nothing here is read by the node that isn't also drawn on screen. Node-local attributes (tier, token state) live in ~/.diplomat/mesh/node.json on each machine; mesh-wide placement overrides are gossiped last-writer-wins and start from the defaults here.
_transportsComment: How an EDGE between two nodes runs. Peers that share a network link over the 'lan' (a direct TCP connection to a LAN address, the path multicast discovery finds); peers that do not link over a WAN transport, which gives each node a permanent, NAT-independent address it advertises inside its signed advert — an iroh endpoint id or a v3 onion (szpontnet-spec/docs/15, /14). Every edge runs over exactly ONE of these, never two: a link is one connection, and the WAN one an edge uses is the most-preferred transport BOTH ends run. That preference is picked mesh-wide from the Mesh screen and gossiped last-writer-wins beside the duty placements ('wan' in the overrides record); it ORDERS, it does not exclude, so a peer that runs only the other transport is still reached over that one — and a pair that shares neither has no way back once they leave the LAN, which is what the screen flags. Preference reorders future dials only: a live link is never torn down to move it.

transports.title: LAN
transports.detail: A direct TCP link to the peer's address on this network

transports.title: Iroh
transports.detail: QUIC to a peer's endpoint id — hole-punched where both networks allow it, relayed where they don't. No daemon, and a dial resolves in well under a second.

transports.title: Tor
transports.detail: A v3 onion service — costs a local tor daemon and a multi-minute bootstrap, and needs nothing installed beyond it.

trust._comment: How much a node trusts a PEER. Trust is NEVER derived from an advertised field (those are spoofable). Each device has an Ed25519 keypair; a peer must sign a fresh per-connection challenge to prove it holds the key it advertises, and trust keys on that verified key's fingerprint against a LOCAL, operator-managed allowlist (~/.diplomat/mesh/trusted.json), never gossiped. 'personal' = the peer's proven fingerprint is in my allowlist → a received SzpontRequest runs directly, as if I'd triggered it locally. 'foreign' = a device I have not marked personal → its requests are declined by default, or — with a confinement runner (SZPONTNET_FOREIGN_SPAWN) configured — run confined and response-only: the compute runs sandboxed and the result is routed back for the requester to act on (never a social action here). See szpontnet-spec/docs/13-foreign-execution.md. 'banned' = a device this node has marked as having broken the foreign-accountability contract (it ACCEPTED a SzpontRequest and failed to deliver its result within the completion deadline, then gave no — or a non-fulfilling — answer to the readiness reminder; see szpontnet-spec/docs/13-foreign-execution.md#accountability-deadline-reminder-ban). Banned is machine-local like the allowlist (~/.diplomat/mesh/banned.json, never gossiped): every request from a banned device is declined outright (even with a confinement runner) and it is never picked as a dispatch target. 'default' is the trust level for an UNKNOWN device (not in the allowlist, or unverified/keyless): it ships 'foreign' (zero-trust by default — a new device is untrusted until the operator promotes it to personal), and can be overridden per-node (SZPONTNET_DEFAULT_TRUST, or the panel's default-trust toggle, persisted in trusted.json). Set it to 'personal' to restore the pre-trust full-altruism mode where every unlisted peer is trusted.

tiers._comment: Machine strength, 1 = strongest. 'weakest-first' keeps the strong machine free for interactive work by routing grunt jobs to the weakest eligible node. Auto-detected CPU-quality-first (Apple-Silicon variant / boost clock, then physical cores, RAM, dGPU — see szpontnet-core/szpontnet/hardware.py); a manual edit in the panel pins it. 'labels' give the UIs human words instead of a bare number.

strategies.title: Weakest first
strategies.detail: route to the weakest eligible machine — keeps the strong ones free

strategies.title: Strongest first
strategies.detail: route to the strongest eligible machine — fastest wall-clock

strategies.title: Local first
strategies.detail: run on the dispatching machine when eligible, else weakest-first

strategies.title: Most surplus first
strategies.detail: route to the node with the most spare quota RELATIVE to its reset — budget left ÷ clock left; ties fall back to weakest-first

_defaultStrategyComment: surplus-first is the default: absent a reason to pin a duty elsewhere, work should follow spare capacity. Surplus is a burn-down RATIO (see accounts._surplusComment in szpontnet-core/szpontnet/netmodel.json), so the ordering is stable — it only moves when a node's standing against its own reset clock genuinely changes, not as raw percentages tick down.

placement._comment: The bundle E2E runs on one Linux AND one macOS node — platform coverage beats machine preference here. No 'strategy' key, so it inherits defaultStrategy (surplus-first): within each platform slot the flusher node wins.
